2027-02-14.title: Garbo Sunday · The Healing of the Leper
readings: Naaman is cleansed in the Jordan
They shall seek the Lord their God
Jesus touches and cleanses a leper
2027-02-14.alt: Second Sunday of the Great Fast.
2027-02-14.verse: Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.
theo: The Sundays of the Great Fast in our tradition follow Christ the physician: the leper, the paralytic, the Canaanite woman's daughter, the bent woman, the man born blind. Lent is a season of healing. Today a man “covered with leprosy” falls on his face before Jesus and says: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” Jesus “stretched out his hand, touched him, and said, ‘I do choose. Be made clean.’ Immediately the leprosy left him.”

Leprosy in the Bible was more than a disease. The leper had to live outside the camp, cry “Unclean!”, and could touch no one. Jesus does what no one would do: he touches him. The Law said that touching a leper made you unclean; with Jesus, the opposite happens: his touch makes the leper clean. This is what Lent offers us: the touch of Christ on the parts of our life we hide from others.

Naaman, the proud Syrian general, was told by Elisha to wash seven times in the Jordan. At first he was angry: was this not too simple? But when he obeyed, “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.” Healing requires humility. The leper in the Gospel knelt; Naaman went down into the river. In Lent we kneel in confession and go down into the waters of repentance.

Isaiah prays: “O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble.” Jesus himself, after healing the leper, “would withdraw to deserted places and pray.” Healing and prayer go together. Let us bring to Christ in this Fast whatever in us is unclean, and hear him say: “I do choose. Be made clean.”
conn: Elisha healed a foreigner through the waters of the Jordan; Jesus heals with a touch and a word. Jesus himself recalls Naaman (Luke 4:27).
Noah entering the ark (Genesis 7) is an image of salvation through the Church and Baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21).
Leviticus 13:45–46 excluded lepers; Christ “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12) to bring the excluded in.
The Fathers saw leprosy as an image of sin: it spreads, isolates and disfigures; only Christ cleanses.
altar: The leper asked to be touched; in Holy Communion Christ does more than touch us: he enters us. Before Communion we say with the centurion and the leper: Lord, I am not worthy, but only say the word.
outline: The Sundays of Lent: Christ the physician.
Humble, trusting prayer. Jesus always chooses to heal what we bring him.
Jesus touches the untouchable. Who are the “lepers” of our society?
Healing through simple obedience: Confession, prayer, fasting.
Jesus withdrew to pray; make space for prayer in Lent.
live: Bring Christ what you hide most; hear the words of absolution as his touch.
Visit or help someone avoided by others: a patient, a migrant worker, a prisoner's family.
Begin each day of the Fast with “O Lord, be our arm every morning.”
fathers: Christ touched the leper to show that he was not under the law but above it, and that to the pure nothing is impure: his hand did not become unclean, but the leprous body became clean (Homilies on Matthew 25).
He calls Christ the Physician who came down to the sick, and asks that the medicine of his mercy heal the hidden sores of the soul (Hymns on the Fast).
magis: Christ the physician: his compassion for the sick and his healings are signs that God has visited his people; he takes up our infirmities.
The Lord Jesus, physician of our souls and bodies, willed that his Church continue his work of healing in the sacraments of Penance and Anointing.
Message for the World Day of the Sick
The Church cares for the sick as Christ did; read the Pope's annual message (11 February) on vatican.va.
saints: The weekdays of the Great Fast. Monday 22 Feb: the Throne of St Peter at Antioch.
2027-02-14.prayer: Lord Jesus, physician of souls and bodies, you touched the leper and made him clean. Stretch out your hand over us in this Fast: cleanse what is hidden, heal what is wounded, and give us the humility of Naaman and the faith of the leper. Amen.

quick: Lent is a season of healing: Christ the physician.
Jesus touches the untouchable and makes him clean.
Healing needs humility: kneel like the leper, wash like Naaman.
2027-02-14.action: Make a good Confession during this week of the Fast.
2027-02-14.question: What “leprosy” in my life am I hiding from Jesus?
2027-02-14.special: Garbo Sunday, second Sunday of the Great Fast.
illus: Kerala once had leprosy hospitals run by religious sisters, who washed and bandaged patients whom even their families had abandoned. Visitors were amazed that the sisters touched them with bare hands. They had learnt it from Jesus.

family.explain: A man with a skin disease called leprosy was alone; nobody would touch him. He asked Jesus for help, and Jesus touched him and healed him.
family.intention: We pray for the sick, and for people who are left alone or rejected.
family.ask: Ask: “Who is lonely at school or at work, and how can we be kind to them?”

kidsaint: A Belgian priest who went to live with people suffering from leprosy on the island of Molokai, cared for them, built homes and a church, and finally caught the disease himself. Lesson: love the people others avoid.
term: Garbo is Syriac for “leper”. The second Sunday of the Great Fast, when the Church reads the healing of the leper. The Sundays of the Fast are named after Christ's healings.
termMore: The Malankara Great Fast follows Christ the physician from Sunday to Sunday: the leper, the paralytic, the Canaanite woman's daughter, the bent woman and the man born blind. Lent is our journey of healing towards Easter.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, in our tradition every Sunday of the Great Fast shows us Christ the physician. Today a leper comes to him. In those days a leper lived outside the village, had to cry “Unclean!” when anyone came near, and could touch no one. This man kneels and says: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”

Then Jesus does something no one else would do. He stretches out his hand and touches him. “I do choose. Be made clean.” By the Law, touching a leper made a person unclean. But with Jesus the opposite happens: his touch makes the leper clean. That is what Lent offers each of us: the touch of Christ on the part of our life we hide from everyone.

Our first reading tells of Naaman, a proud Syrian general with leprosy. The prophet told him simply to wash seven times in the Jordan. He was offended: is that all? But when he humbled himself and obeyed, his flesh became like a child's. Healing needs humility. For us, the Jordan is the sacrament of Confession. It seems too simple. But it heals.

After healing the leper, Jesus withdrew to deserted places to pray. Let us make room for prayer in this Fast, make a good Confession, and reach out to the “lepers” of our time: the sick, the lonely, those everyone avoids. And let us hear Jesus say to us: “I do choose. Be made clean.” Amen.
kids: Children, long ago people with a skin disease called leprosy had to live alone. Nobody would touch them or play with them.
One day a man with leprosy came to Jesus and said: “If you want, you can heal me.” Jesus touched him and said: “I want to. Be healed!” And he was healed!
Is there someone at school whom nobody plays with? Be kind to them, like Jesus. Let's say: “Jesus, make me kind!”

intro: Theme: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”

The Great Fast leads us through Sundays of healing. The first is the leper: a man shut out of community, who dares to come to Jesus. Leprosy is an image of sin, which isolates us from God and from one another.

sub: The Law made the leper live alone, outside the camp.
Sin does the same: it breaks our communion with God, family and Church.
The leper does not hide; he falls on his face before Jesus and asks.
q: He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease; he is unclean. He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp.
There was a man covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he bowed with his face to the ground and begged him, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
points.apply: Name the sin that isolates you, and bring it humbly to the Lord.

sub: No one touched lepers; Jesus stretches out his hand and touches him.
His answer is clear: “I do choose.” God wants our healing.
The Psalmist knows the connection: “heal me, for I have sinned against you.”
q: As for me, I said, “O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you.”
Then Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said, “I do choose. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him.
points.apply: Reach out this week to someone others avoid: the sick, the shamed, the lonely.

sub: Naaman wanted a dramatic cure; he was told simply to wash in the Jordan.
When he obeyed, his flesh became like a child's.
Jesus sends the healed man to the priest: today Christ heals our sins through the priest in Confession.
q: So he went down and immersed himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God; his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.
“Go,” he said, “and show yourself to the priest, and, as Moses commanded, make an offering for your cleansing, for a testimony to them.”
points.apply: Make a good confession during this Great Fast.

concl: What the leper said, we can say: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
Christ chooses. Let us come to him, let him touch us, and go home clean.
2027-02-14.resolve: Prepare an examination of conscience this week and go to confession.
